blocks.text: In Turkey you will see it everywhere: a flat glass bead with rings of dark blue, white and pale blue around a dark centre, like an eye looking back at you. This is the *nazar boncuğu*, the evil-eye bead.

*Nazar* is the evil eye: the belief that an envious look, or even an admiring one, can bring bad luck to whatever it falls on, such as a newborn baby, a new home or a success. The bead is there to meet that look first. When one cracks, people say it has done its job and absorbed a strong *nazar*, and they put up a new one.

The belief is much older than modern Turkey and is shared around the Mediterranean and the Middle East. Eye beads go back to the early days of glassmaking: examples survive from as early as the 16th century BCE, and glass beads like them were made in Mesopotamia, Egypt, Phoenicia, Greece and Rome.

Today the bead is part of everyday life. It is one of the most common gifts for a newborn, and it is often pinned out of sight on a baby's clothes. It hangs on walls and doors at home, and the eye pattern decorates bracelets, earrings, plates and towels. In 2018 it even became an emoji.

Traditional beads are still made by hand in a few villages near İzmir, on the Aegean coast. Görece, south of the city, has had a registered geographical indication for its beads since 2005, and the village of Kurudere, in the district of Kemalpaşa, has been renamed *Nazarköy*: evil-eye village.

The work starts early in the morning at a kiln fired with pine wood, which heats the glass to around 1,000 °C. The master winds a blob of molten glass around a steel rod, then presses on the eye one colour at a time; copper is what gives the pale blue its tint. The finished beads go into a cooler chamber and lose their heat slowly, or they would crack.
When someone admires a baby or a new car, Turkish speakers often add *nazar değmesin*: may the evil eye not touch it.
